Later, they learned that the feathers and other organs of the pitohui were found to contain batrachotoxin. Since then, six other songbirds in PNG have been found to possess the same toxin in varying amounts.
Papua New Guinea's top predator is the New Guinea harpy eagle (Harpyopsis novaeguineae). PNG shares with the Philippines and New Zealand the distinction of having this bird as top predator.
Most seabirds' native to PNG i s found throughout the tropics. Although some species are hunted for meat, valuable plumes and feathers, or for the pet trade, the main threats to most species come from logging and conversion of forest for agriculture, both of which degrade or eliminate important habitat.
The birds-of-paradise are members of the family Paradisaeidae of the order Passeriformes. The majority of species are found in Papua New Guinea . The family has 42 species in 15 genera. The members of this family are perhaps best known for the plumage of the males of the species (the majority) which are sexually dimorphic, in particular the very long elaborate feathers extending from the beak, wings, tail or head. For the most part they are confined to dense rainforest habitat. The diet of all species is dominated by fruit and to a lesser extent arthropods. The birds -of-paradise have a variety of breeding systems, ranging from monogamy to lek-type polygamy.
A number of species are threatened by hunting and habitat loss.

text:
The amplified sound exits the stapes and connects to the oval window that connects the middle ear to the inner ear. - 3. Inner Ear
From the oval window, the sound waves enter the inner ear and then into a snail-shaped organ called the cochlea. The cochlea is filled with a fluid that moves in response to the vibrations from the oval window. As the fluid moves, thousands of nerve endings (about 25,000) are set into motion. These nerve endings transform the vibrations into electrical impulses that then travel along the eighth cranial nerve (auditory nerve) to the brain. The brain then interprets these signals, and this is how we hear. The inner ear also contains the vestibular organ that is responsible for balance.
1.2.2.2. Mechanism of the Hearing Aid
A hearing aid is like a mini-PA system that has three basic parts: a microphone, amplifier, and speaker. The hearing aid receives sound through the microphone. Most hearing aids use two microphones to help cancel out background noise. The microphone performs two functions; it captures the sound and converts them into electric signals.
The sound-to electric conversion occurs within a section of the microphone containing the diaphragm. This is a small and thin plastic that acts like the eardrum, moving back and forth as the sound waves come into contact. A coil attached to the diaphragm a nd a permanent magnet is also forced to oscillate, generating electric current or signals through electromagnetic induction. The electric signals then flow to an amplifier that then increases the power of the current and then sends them through the ear to the speaker.

This is a part of biological brains that is required to coordinate fine motor movements. The CMAC model forms complex nonlinear maps adaptively and has been used in a number of robotic applications.
The Marr neocortex model is an example of an attempt to determine the function of cell layers in the neocortex, as is the Kurogi spatiotemporal pattern recognition model. Kurogi's model is unique among high-level models in that it is one of the few to model internal neuron dynamics and specify how nerve action potentials are generated and processed on a spikeby-spike basis. Most other models include variables that represent the average cell firing rate. This is a neurobiological model which makes predictions whose details can be tested by neurobiologists.
The upper third of Fig.SP-AI-SRB-3.8 includes models that are trained without supervision or with self-supervision. The three left-most networks vector-quantize the inputs and form
clusters. Competitive learning networks form internal clusters from binary inputs while Kohonen's feature map forms clusters from continuous valued inputs. Both networks form clusters using a fixed number of nodes and a sequential algorithm similar in purpose to the conventional k-means clustering algorithm. The feature map algorithm is unique in that nodes representing clusters become arranged in a two-dimensional spatial grid or map where nearby nodes respond to stimuli with similar characteristics. The adaptive resonance theory (ART) clustering algorithm forms a new cluster whenever an input is too far from an already existing cluster.

text:
Feature | Prokaryotic Genes | Eukaryotic Genes
Arrangement | Continuous coding sequence | Split into exons and introns
Introns | Usually, absent | Usually, present
RNA Processing | Minimal | Extensive splicing required
Alternative Splicing | Rare | Common
Protein Products | Usually, one gene → one protein | One gene may produce multiple proteins
Why is Alternative Splicing Important?
Alternative splicing increases genetic efficiency by allowing a single gene to produce different protein variants. This contributes to the complexity of higher organisms and enables cells to produce proteins that are specialized for different functions and tissues.
As a result, alternative splicing plays an important role in growth, development, adaptation, and cellular diversity.

Figure 4: Eukaryotic genes are split into exons and introns; alternative splicing lets one gene make several proteins.

text:
The Calvin cycle depends on the products of the light-dependent reactions:
- ATP supplies the energy required for the reactions.
- NADPH provides high-energy electrons and hydrogen needed to reduce carbon dioxide and form sugars.
Without ATP and NADPH, carbon dioxide could not be converted into glucose.
Summary of the Calvin Cycle
Phase | Main Event
Carbon Fixation | CO₂ combines with RuBP through the action of rubisco
Reduction | ATP and NADPH convert the products into G3P
Regeneration | RuBP is regenerated so the cycle can continue
The Calvin cycle ultimately converts inorganic carbon dioxide into organic molecules that can be used to produce glucose, providing the chemical energy and building materials required for plant growth and development.
Although the Calvin cycle does not directly require light, it remains dependent on the ATP and NADPH generated during the light-dependent reactions. For this reason, both stages of photosynthesis are closely interconnected and work together to produce glucose.
Figure 4: The Calvin cycle - carbon fixation, reduction and regeneration of RuBP in the stroma.

text:
- Central dogma - The flow of genetic information: DNA → RNA → protein.
- Gene expression - Using a gene's information to make a functional product.
- Transcription - Copying a gene into messenger RNA (mRNA).
- RNA polymerase - The enzyme that builds mRNA from a DNA template.
- Template strand - The DNA strand that is read during transcription.
Teacher notes: Central dogma - The flow of genetic information: DNA → RNA → protein.

text:
- Three kinds of RNA do the work:
- mRNA (messenger): carries the coded message from the DNA in the nucleus to the ribosome.
- tRNA (transfer): brings the correct amino acid to match each codon.
- rRNA (ribosomal): makes up the ribosome, the machine that builds the protein.
- Figure 1: The three types of RNA work together to convert genetic information into proteins.
Teacher notes: Gene expression is the whole process of using the information in a gene to make a functional product (usually a protein). Although every cell has the same DNA, different genes are switched on or off in different cells - which is why a nerve cell and a skin cell are so different.
